passage:
When I started freelancing, I thought negotiating meant hiding everything and squeezing the other side. The deal with Arnab's company taught me otherwise.
Arnab ran a small ed-tech firm and wanted illustrations for forty lessons. He offered a rate lower than I'd hoped. I told him the truth: "The rate matters less to me than being paid on time. Last year two clients paid four months late and I had to borrow from my sister."
Then I asked, "What matters most to you?"
He thought. "Speed. We launch in August, and our last illustrator vanished."
So we built the deal around that. I'd deliver in weekly batches; he'd pay each batch within seven days. I took his rate, but with a bonus if we hit August.
We did. It's been two years. Neither of us has ever had to chase the other.
Ishita

qa.q: How many lessons did Arnab want illustrations for?
qa.a: Arnab wanted illustrations for forty lessons.

qa.q: How might Ishita have felt telling Arnab about the late payments?
qa.a: Ishita likely felt a little exposed sharing the borrowing, but chose honesty, wanting terms built on the real need to be paid on time rather than a fight over the rate.

qa.q: Which question helped the negotiation most?
qa.a: Asking "What matters most to you?" revealed Arnab's need for speed, which let them design weekly batches, quick payment and a bonus for August.

qa.q: How might Arnab see the deal after two years?
qa.a: Arnab probably trusts Ishita as a reliable collaborator, since the honest terms meant neither of them has ever had to chase the other.

grounding: Ishita negotiates by stating needs truthfully and asking what matters to Arnab, and they build terms that work for both and last.

passage:
Procurement review note. Written by Gautam, purchase head, 22 August.
I sat in on Santosh's first supplier negotiation today, for the packaging order. He is twenty-five and has been with us eight months.
I expected him to push on price, as juniors usually do. Instead he opened by telling the supplier plainly that our real problem was late deliveries in the festival season, not cost. Then he asked, "What makes our orders difficult for you?"
The supplier admitted our last-minute size changes caused most of their delays. Santosh offered to freeze sizes six weeks in advance. In return the supplier agreed to guaranteed festival-season dates and a small discount.
Both sides left relaxed. Nobody was bluffing.
Next steps: I have asked Santosh to write up his approach for the team meeting, and I will propose we adopt the six-week size freeze across all packaging orders.

qa.q: How far ahead did Santosh offer to freeze sizes?
qa.a: Santosh offered to freeze sizes six weeks in advance.

qa.q: What does Gautam's note suggest about Gautam's feelings watching Santosh?
qa.a: Gautam expected a junior to push hard on price, so Gautam seems pleasantly surprised and impressed that Santosh chose honesty and curiosity instead.

qa.q: What made Santosh's negotiation work for both sides?
qa.a: He named the company's real need truthfully, asked what made orders difficult for the supplier, and traded a size freeze for reliable dates.

qa.q: How might the supplier feel about working with this company now?
qa.a: The supplier likely feels heard and less stressed, since the fix for last-minute changes makes their work easier, so they may want to keep the deal.

grounding: A purchase head records a junior buyer who explains needs truthfully, asks what matters to the supplier, and finds terms that work for both.

passage:
Saturday
Rent renewal talk with Ujjwal uncle today. I was dreading it.
Instead of arguing, I just told him the truth: I work from home, I love the flat, and a big jump would push me to move. Then I asked him, "What matters most to you?"
He thought for a bit. He said his last tenants paid late and called him about every dripping tap, and he's tired of chasing. He wants someone steady so he doesn't have to worry from Nagpur.
So we worked it out. A smaller increase, a two-year agreement, rent on the 1st by bank transfer, and I'll handle small repairs myself and send him photos. He even offered to fix the geyser first.
It felt like we were solving one problem together, not fighting over one pie.
I think this one will actually last.
Ira

qa.q: What was Ujjwal uncle tired of with the last tenants?
qa.a: They paid late and called him about every dripping tap.

qa.q: How did Ira feel before and after the talk?
qa.a: Ira was dreading it beforehand and came away relieved and hopeful, feeling they had solved one problem together.

qa.q: Which choices made the deal fair for both?
qa.a: Ira told the truth about needs, asked what mattered to Ujjwal uncle, and they traded a smaller increase for a two-year agreement, rent on the 1st and Ira handling small repairs.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal uncle gain from the deal?
qa.a: Ujjwal uncle gets a steady tenant, rent on the 1st and fewer calls about taps, so there is less to worry about from Nagpur.

grounding: Shows a tenant explaining real needs, asking what matters to the landlord, and reaching terms that work for both.

passage:
In the small town of Nahan, Himani's family dairy had four cows and one problem: the milk collection centre paid late. Sarita, who ran the busiest sweet shop near the bus stand, wanted fresh milk every morning.
"Tell me your real need first," Sarita said, pouring tea behind the counter.
Himani took a breath. "I need payment every week, not every month. Feed costs come every week. I can't bargain like the big dairies."
Sarita nodded. "And I need milk that doesn't run short in wedding season, when I make three times the sweets."
They sat with a notebook. Himani would keep aside extra milk from November to February, even if it meant selling less to neighbours. Sarita would pay every Saturday, and a little more per litre in the wedding months.
They wrote it down, both signed, and Sarita's son made a copy on his phone.
A year later the notebook page was soft from folding, and neither had missed a Saturday.

qa.q: On which day would Sarita pay?
qa.a: Sarita would pay every Saturday.

qa.q: How did Himani feel explaining the real need?
qa.a: Himani felt nervous, taking a breath before admitting the family can't bargain like big dairies, but was honest about needing weekly payments.

qa.q: What made this deal easier to keep?
qa.a: Both stated their real needs, planned around wedding season and weekly payments, and wrote it down with both signatures and a copy.

qa.q: What mattered most to Sarita in the deal?
qa.a: Sarita needed milk that wouldn't run short in wedding season, when she makes three times the sweets.

grounding: Shows two small-town traders stating real needs, asking what matters to the other, and building terms that last.

passage: Bao had run his small café in Hanoi for three years when he finally met Abebe, the coffee exporter, at a trade fair in Da Nang. Bao could have played it cool. Instead he said plainly, "I can't pay more than I pay now, this year. I'm a small shop. But I want your beans for a long time, not one order." Abebe raised an eyebrow. "Most buyers pretend they have five other suppliers." "I have one other, and theirs are worse," Bao laughed. "What matters most to you?" Abebe thought. "Steady orders. Our farmers need to know in advance." They sat over two cups for an hour. In the end Bao agreed to a fixed monthly order for two years, and Abebe offered a price Bao could manage, rising a little each year. They wrote it down together. A year later, when a drought pushed prices up everywhere, Abebe's shipments to the café still arrived on time.

qa.q: Where did Bao meet Abebe?
qa.a: At a trade fair in Da Nang.

qa.q: How did Abebe seem to feel about Bao's honesty?
qa.a: Abebe seemed surprised and intrigued, raising an eyebrow, since most buyers pretend to have many suppliers.

qa.q: What made the deal work for both of them?
qa.a: Bao explained his real limits and asked what mattered to Abebe; a fixed monthly order for two years gave the farmers steady orders and Bao a price he could manage.

qa.q: What would change if Bao had bluffed about five suppliers?
qa.a: Abebe might have held back or charged more, and the trust that kept shipments coming through the drought might never have formed.

grounding: Shows a negotiator explaining needs truthfully, asking what matters to the other side, and building terms that work for both and last.
